1.7 Functor categories

Given two categories \(C\) and \(D\), we are interested in forming the functor category \(\Fun (C,D)\) whose objects are precisely the functors from \(C\) to \(D\).

Given any functor \(e \colon F \times C\to D\) and any category \(T\), we can form a functor \[ \mathit {u}_T\colon \Map (T,F)\to \Map (T\times C,D) \] by currying the composite \[ \Map (T,F)\times T\times C \xrightarrow {\ev _{\Map } \times \id _C} F\times C\xrightarrow {e} D. \] It satisfies the property that it evaluations on an absolute object of \(\Map (T,F)\), corresponding to a functor \(g\colon T\to F\), as \[ \mathit {u}_T(g)= e\circ (g\times \id _C). \]

    evaluation-forward : MAP (Map T F) (Map (T × C) D)
Proof / implementation
    evaluation-forward = mapCurry (map-isAn T F) evaluation-universal

Definition 1.7.1. A functor category from \(C\) to \(D\) is a category \(F\) equipped with a functor \(e\colon F\times C\to D\) such that, for any category \(T\), the induced map \[ \mathit {u}_T\colon \Map (T,F)\iso \Map (T\times C,D) \] is an equivalence. We then call \(F\) the category of functors from \(C\) to \(D\) and \(e\) the evaluation functor.

Agda The universal property of a functor category

Proof / implementation

Proposition 1.7.2. If \(F\) and \(F'\) both are categories of functors from \(C\) to \(D\) with evaluation functors \(e\) and \(e'\) respectively, then there is an equivalence \(\varphi \colon F'\iso F\) as well as \(\sigma \colon e\circ (\varphi \times \id _C)= e'\).

Agda Uniqueness of functor categories

functor-category-comparison-isEquiv

Derivation, checked

  functor-category-comparison-isEquiv : IsEquiv functor-category-comparison
Proof / implementation
  functor-category-comparison-isEquiv = record
    { inverse = back; left-inverse-law = left ⁻¹; right-inverse-law = right ⁻¹ }
    where
    back : MAP G F
    back = curry e u d
    left : (back ∘ functor-category-comparison) =₁ id F
    left = reflect e u _ _
      ((evaluate-id e) ⁻¹ ∙
        (functor-category-comparison-β ∙
          ((curry-β e u d ▷ productMap functor-category-comparison (id C)) ∙
            evaluate-restrict e back functor-category-comparison)))
    right : (functor-category-comparison ∘ back) =₁ id G
    right = reflect d v _ _
      ((evaluate-id d) ⁻¹ ∙
        (curry-β e u d ∙
          ((functor-category-comparison-β ▷ productMap back (id C)) ∙
            evaluate-restrict d functor-category-comparison back)))

Proof

Proof. Let \(v\) be an inverse of the equivalence \(u_{F'}\colon \Map (F',F)\iso \Map (F'\times C,D)\) and define \(\varphi :=v(e')\colon F'\to F\). By Construction 1.4.1, the identification \(u_{F'}\circ v=\id \) and the beta comparison for \(u_{F'}\) provide \[ \sigma \colon e\circ (\varphi \times \id _C)= e'. \] Exchanging the roles of \((F,e)\) and \((F',e')\), we similarly obtain a functor \(\psi \colon F\to F'\) together with \(e'\circ (\psi \times \id _C)= e\). Combining the two, the uncurried functors associated to \(\varphi \circ \psi \) and \(\id _F\) are identified: \[ e\circ ((\varphi \circ \psi )\times \id _C) = e'\circ (\psi \times \id _C) = e = e\circ (\id _F\times \id _C). \] Since \(u_F\) is an equivalence, it reflects this identification and gives \(\varphi \circ \psi =\id _F\). The same argument shows \(\psi \circ \varphi =\id _{F'}\), so \(\varphi \) is an equivalence with inverse \(\psi \). □

Agda Constructing the comparison functor

Axiom B.8 (Functor category). For any two categories \(C\) and \(D\), there is a category \(\Fun (C, D)\) equipped with an evaluation functor \(\ev \colon \Fun (C,D) \times C \to D\) that exhibits it as a functor category from \(C\) to \(D\).

Definition 1.7.3. Given another category \(T\), choose an inverse \(v_T\) of the equivalence \(\mathit {u}_T\). For a functor \(f\colon T\times C\to D\), define its currying by applying \(v_T\): \[ f_c:=v_T(f)\colon T\longrightarrow \Fun (C,D). \] It comes equipped with a commutative diagram as follows:

Conversely, given a functor \(g\colon T \to \Fun (C,D)\), we call the composite \[ T \times C \xrightarrow {g \times \id _C} \Fun (C,D) \times C \xrightarrow {\ev } D \] the uncurrying of \(g\) and denote it by \(g^u\). The discussion before shows it is identified with \(\mathit {u}_T(g)\). Similarly, an identification \(\beta \colon g= h\) induces an identification \(\beta ^u\colon g^u= h^u\). At the level of mapping animae, uncurrying is the equivalence \[ (-)^u \colon \Map (T,\Fun (C,D))\iso \Map (T\times C,D) \] with inverse defined by currying.

1.7.1 Properties of functor categories

The universal property of functor categories allows us to deduce their compatibilities with the terminal category, the initial category, products, coproducts and pullbacks from the corresponding properties of mapping animae. For every category \(T\), the universal property of functor categories and Proposition 1.4.5 give equivalences \[ \begin {aligned} \Map (T,\Fun (C,D\times E)) &\simeq \Map (T\times C,D\times E)\\ &\simeq \Map (T\times C,D)\times \Map (T\times C,E)\\ &\simeq \Map (T,\Fun (C,D))\times \Map (T,\Fun (C,E))\\ &\simeq \Map (T,\Fun (C,D)\times \Fun (C,E)). \end {aligned} \] This composite is induced by the functor in the statement: after uncurrying, its two components are postcomposition with \(\pr _1\) and \(\pr _2\), by Lemma 1.7.7. The result follows from Proposition 1.4.11. □

Proof

Proof. By Proposition 1.6.3, it suffices to show that the pullback square defining \(C \times _E D\) remains a pullback square after applying \(\Map (S,\Fun (T,-))\) for every category \(S\). Under uncurrying, its four corners are identified with \[ \Map (S\times T,C\times _E D),\quad \Map (S\times T,C),\quad \Map (S\times T,D),\quad \Map (S\times T,E). \] By Lemma 1.7.7, the four functors become postcomposition with the original projections, \(f\), and \(g\). These comparisons respect the specified commutativity identification, as follows by uncurrying its defining postcomposition identification. We conclude that this square agrees with the one obtained by applying \(\Map (S \times T, -)\) to the original pullback square, including its commutativity data. So the resulting square is a pullback by Proposition 1.6.3. □

Proof

Proof. We define the preferred functor as the curried functor of the following composite: \[ \Fun (C,\Fun (D,E)) \times C \times D \xrightarrow {\ev \times \id _{D}} \Fun (D,E) \times D \xrightarrow {\ev } E. \] To construct an inverse, it will by currying suffice to construct a functor \(\Fun (C \times D,E) \times C \to \Fun (D,E)\), which we may take to be the curried functor of the following composite \[ \Fun (C \times D,E) \times C \times D \xrightarrow {\ev } E. \] By construction, these two functors are compatible with the chain of equivalences \begin {align*} \Map (T,\Fun (C,\Fun (D,E))) &\simeq \Map (T\times C,\Fun (D,E))\\ &\simeq \Map ((T\times C)\times D,E)\\ &\simeq \Map (T\times (C\times D),E)\\ &\simeq \Map (T,\Fun (C\times D,E))\, . \end {align*}

Proof

Proof. For every category \(T\), there are equivalences \[ \begin {aligned} \Map (T,\Fun (C\sqcup D,E)) &\simeq \Map (T\times (C\sqcup D),E)\\ &\simeq \Map ((T\times C)\sqcup (T\times D),E)\\ &\simeq \Map (T\times C,E)\times \Map (T\times D,E)\\ &\simeq \Map (T,\Fun (C,E))\times \Map (T,\Fun (D,E))\\ &\simeq \Map (T,\Fun (C,E)\times \Fun (D,E)), \end {aligned} \] using distributivity, the coproduct axiom, and Proposition 1.4.5. This composite is induced by \((i_C^*,i_D^*)\): after uncurrying, its components are restriction along \(T\times i_C\) and \(T\times i_D\), which correspond under Corollary 1.6.17 to the two coproduct inclusions. The result follows from Proposition 1.4.11. □

1.7.2 Mapping animae and functor categories

Proof

Proof. The universal property of functor categories gives equivalences \[ \Fun (C,D)^\simeq =\Map (*,\Fun (C,D)) \simeq \Map (*\times C,D) \simeq \Map (C,D). \] The inverse of their composite is the desired equivalence. To check compatibility with the canonical functors, it suffices to uncurry. Both resulting functors \(\Map (C,D)\times C\to D\) are identified with mapping-anima evaluation. □
